images.alt: Line drawings of seven spear heads: a bound barb, a row of stingray barbs, single and multiple stingray points, a four-pronged fish spear, an acicular spear with two barbs, and a quartz-edged tip
images.caption: Roth's spear heads, 1909. Fig. 3: a barb bound on with twine, ending in a plain looping (Pennefather). Fig. 4: multiple stingray barbs 'placed one behind the other', the Bloomfield dikarra. Figs. 5 and 6: single and multiple stingray-pointed spears of Cape Bedford, Princess Charlotte Bay, the Bloomfield and the middle Palmer, the dajal. Fig. 7: the four-pronged fish spear, each prong with a single barb, the yinba. Fig. 9: the tip 'mounted with quartz flakes on both sides', the kuyan. Fig. 8 is a Rockhampton spear. Public domain.
images.credit: Drawing: D. B. Fry after W. E. Roth, Records of the Australian Museum 7(4), 1909, Plate LVIII (figs 3–9); scan by the Australian Museum

images.alt: Line drawings of spear-thrower pegs and handles: a shell-hafted thrower, pegs tied through drilled holes, a plain handle, a shell handle, a bent-lath handle, and a curved moon-shaped thrower
images.caption: Roth's woomeras, 1909. Fig. 15: a Pennefather thrower hafted with two pieces of baler shell. Figs. 17 and 18: the middle Palmer and Laura peg, long, flattened, drilled and tied through the blade, with the back of the peg left clear of cement. Figs. 19 and 20: the Cape Bedford, Bloomfield and Butcher's Hill peg, tied through two holes in the blade only, then cemented over. Figs. 21 to 23: the same thrower's handle, haftless, hafted with baler shell in beeswax, or with a thin lath bent on itself. Fig. 24: the moon-shaped haftless ballur of the Bloomfield River. Public domain.
images.credit: Drawing: D. B. Fry after W. E. Roth, Records of the Australian Museum 7(4), 1909, Plate LVIII (figs 15–24); scan by the Australian Museum

images.alt: A spreading tree beside a road in dry country
images.caption: Cooktown ironwood, jujabala: the blade of the straight hunting woomera, a spear-point wood and a root gum. It grows across Western Yalanji country.

images.alt: A tall slender palm with a bushy, bottlebrush-like crown against a mountain and blue sky
images.caption: Black palm, duwar, the Bloomfield spear wood: its hard trunk was split into tips, long shafts and prongs. It is a rainforest palm and does not grow inland.
images.credit: Photo: Steve Fitzgerald, via Wikimedia Commons

images.alt: A tall green flower spike of a grass tree covered in small white flowers
images.caption: A grass-tree flower spike, nganjirr. Once it is dead and dry it is the light, straight butt of the hunting spear and the fish spear, and the resin among the roots is the pitch, kanunjul.
images.credit: Photo: Steve Fitzgerald, via Wikimedia Commons

images.alt: Silvery wattle foliage with rod-like flower spikes in bud
images.caption: Candelabra wattle, one of the common wattles on the station. Wattle made the short hardwood tips with a wooden barb, the fire-hardened turtle point kurrajan, and the long woomera peg of the middle Palmer.

images.alt: Dark glossy oval leaves of a small tree
images.caption: Quinine bush, Petalostigma: the wood of the short nicked peg on the Cape Bedford, Bloomfield and Butcher's Hill woomera.
images.credit: Photo: Ethel Aardvark, via Wikimedia Commons

images.alt: The dark, deeply fissured bark of a beefwood trunk
images.caption: Beefwood, Grevillea striata. The sticky bark of its young roots, scraped, baked in tea-tree bark and hammered between greased stones, was 'the strongest and most durable' of the cements and the one preferred over a woomera peg.
images.credit: Photo: Ethel Aardvark, via Wikimedia Commons

images.alt: A full plate of line drawings of spears, spear heads and spear-throwers numbered 1 to 24
images.caption: The whole of Roth's Plate LVIII, 1909: spears of the Wellesley Islands, the Pennefather, Cape Bedford, the Bloomfield and the Palmer, the Rockhampton and Westwood hand spears, and the spear-throwers from the hooked stick of the Wellesley Islands to the ballur of the Bloomfield. Public domain.
images.credit: Drawing: D. B. Fry after W. E. Roth, Records of the Australian Museum 7(4), 1909, Plate LVIII; scan by the Australian Museum

images.alt: Watercolour of a plain wooden spear and a flat spear-thrower lying on red earth
images.caption: A hunting spear with a resin-sealed binding, and a spear-thrower whose peg hook fits the spear's butt. Illustration based on the descriptions on this page.
